chunks: Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Hammad ibn Isa, from Hariz, from one of the two (peace be upon them), who said:

Amir al-Mu'minin (peace be upon him) judged in Yemen regarding a people upon whom a house of theirs had collapsed, so two young children remained from them, one of them a slave and the other free. So he drew lots between the two of them, and the lot fell upon one of them, so he made the wealth for him and emancipated the other.
ai.seo_question: How did Imam Ali rule on inheritance when a slave and a free person survived a disaster together?
ai.summary: This ruling from Imam Ali’s (peace be upon him) time in Yemen illustrates the principle of *al-khum* (equal division) applied to simultaneous death (*al-mutawaffayan*), where the uncertainty of who died first is resolved by chance. By assigning the estate to one child and using it to free the other, the Imam ensured that both heirs received their full share of the wealth and status, a method later debated by jurists regarding whether the estate should be split directly or via this lottery mechanism. This narrative highlights the practical wisdom (*hikmah*) of the Imam in resolving complex inheritance ambiguities with equitable outcomes.

en.hubeali:
Ali Bin Ibrahim, from his father, from Hammad Bin Isa, from Hareyz, 
(It has been narrated) from one of the two (5<sup>th</sup> or 6<sup>th</sup> Imam<sup>asws</sup>) having said:

‘Amir Al-Momineen<sup>asws</sup> judged at Al-Yemen regarding one people upon whom a house of theirs had collapsed. So there remained two young children, one of them being a slave, the other a free one. So he<sup>asws</sup> drew lots between the two of them, so the lot came upon one of the two, so he<sup>asws</sup> made the wealth to be for him, and emancipated (liberated) the other one’.
en.sarwar: 4. Ali ibn Ibrahim has narrated from his father from Hammad ibn ‘Isa from Hariz who has narrated the following: “One of the two Imam, (abu Ja‘far or abu ‘Abd Allah), ‘Alayhim al-Salam, has said that

Amir al- Mu’minin issued a judgment in Yemen about a people on whom a house had collapsed and only two children were left, of whom one was owned and the other was free. He (the Imam) by means of raffle gave the assets to the one whose name came out and set the other one free.’”
